Independent proof check of transported chords by deleting a transposition and small-step multiplicity control
correctness.rationale: The rank-one midpoint factor is the stated convex two-site update at finite h. Positive diagonal entries and a positive sweep transition for each original oriented tree edge imply irreducibility and aperiodicity, so the zero-sum radius is strictly below one. Starting with singleton cycles, every edge joins different components of a growing forest, and the transposition merges their cycles; the limiting P is one n-cycle. Writing s=1/h gives P⁻¹M=I−sH+O(s²) with H the sum of the transported incidence outer products divided by rates. Differentiating each simple eigenvalue of P gives −ζ_k u_k*Hu_k, and the normalized cycle Fourier vectors give the displayed sine-square formula. If any nonconstant mode had zero first-order attenuation, it would be fixed by all the transported transpositions and therefore by P, a contradiction. As a check on the path and star simplifications, omitting edge j from P multiplies it on the right by its transported transposition; this splits P into cycles of lengths d_j and n−d_j. The two cycles are the components after deleting the original edge. Thus a path has split sizes j and n−j (the sine-square sum is n/2), whereas all star splits are 1 and n−1. For small h the scaled matrix (I−M)/h is L_T+O(h); since the baseline L_T is symmetric, its eigenvalues cluster within O(h) of those of L_T, with the appropriate multiplicities, giving the stated spectral-radius expansions even for the repeated star eigenvalue. For n≥4 the connectivity ordering is opposite to the ordering of the stiff deficits. Continuity on the fixed zero-sum space gives at least one crossover, not uniqueness.
residual_risks: The expansion assumes fixed finite graph, rates and sweep order; it is not uniform in size or rates. Spectral radius controls asymptotic sweep convergence, not one-step singular norm. The frozen numerical tests are illustrative, not the all-tree proof.

value.rationale: The result quantifies how a strictly mixing algorithm approaches a nonmixing permutation in the stiff regime; the coefficient explains precisely why an ordering suggested by continuous-time connectivity can reverse for the completed discrete sweep. The formula treats arbitrary positive rates on every finite tree, not just an isolated numerical crossover.
residual_risks: The comparison is of asymptotic spectral mixing factors; it is not a universal finite-sweep ranking or a prediction of the exact crossover timestep.
